statement: At least three world regions are well documented as having no indigenous writing system before external contact: (1) pre-contact Aboriginal Australia — mainstream consensus holds message sticks and notched digging sticks are graphic/mnemonic communication (Piers Kelly, Australian Message Stick Database, Journal of Material Culture, 2020) rather than writing proper, with no rigorous named-scholar causal explanation for the absence found at citation quality this session; (2) most pre-colonial sub-Saharan Africa outside the Nile Valley, the Ethiopian highlands (Ge'ez), and the West African cases documented separately (Ajami, Nsibidi, and the 19th-20th century Vai/Bamum/N'Ko inventions) — confirmed specifically for Southern African Bantu-speaking societies, with the caveat that a modern invented script for Southern Bantu languages (isiBheqe Sohlamvu/Ditema tsa Dinoko) was created by South African linguists starting c. 2015, analogous to Bamum/Vai/N'Ko, not evidence of pre-colonial tradition; (3) North America north of Mesoamerica — no native writing system existed at first European contact, with post-contact inventions (most famously Sequoyah's Cherokee syllabary) representing informed invention, not indigenous continuity. The distinction between "adapted an outside script" (Ajami, Ge'ez, Meroitic-from-Egyptian) and "no writing system used at all" is the one worth encoding — conflating them (as some polemical sources do) would reproduce the kind of overclaim this project's standing rules are built to avoid, in the other direction.

sources.citation: Kelly, Piers. "Australian message sticks: Old questions, new directions." Journal of Material Culture, 2020.
sources.author: Piers Kelly

sources.citation: Britannica-sourced consensus on absence of pre-contact writing in North America outside Mesoamerica.

does_not_demonstrate: That the absence of indigenous writing implies an absence of sophisticated knowledge-transmission systems (oral tradition, song-line, and mnemonic systems in these regions are independently well documented and are not lesser substitutes)
notes: Some search results for "sub-Saharan Africa no writing" surfaced polemical sources arguing the framing is itself a colonial myth; these were not relied on for factual claims, per the flag in the underlying research report.
